html:
The imperial mosque of Sultan Ahmed I, built from 1609 to 1617 on the southeast side of the old Hippodrome of Istanbul, facing Hagia Sophia. Ahmed was the first sultan to build an imperial mosque since Selim II, whose Selimiye Mosque stands in Edirne. He had won no great war, and the ulema protested that a sultan should pay for such a mosque only from the spoils of conquest. He built it anyway, from the treasury. Its architect, Sedefkar Mehmed Agha, was a pupil of Mimar Sinan.

The plan follows Sinan's Şehzade Mosque: a central dome 23.5 m wide and 43 m high on four huge round pillars, with a half dome on each side. Six minarets stand at the corners of the prayer hall and of the large courtyard. The story that the architect misheard "golden minarets" (altın) as "six minarets" (altı) is a legend. Inside, more than 21,000 Iznik tiles in over fifty designs line the lower walls; in 1613 Ahmed banned the sale of Iznik tiles for any other purpose so that his orders would be filled. The blue paintwork above them gives the mosque its popular name, though much of it is later repainting. About 260 windows light the hall.

Ahmed died in 1617, around the time the mosque opened, and lies in a domed tomb beside it with his wife Kösem and his sons Osman II and Murad IV. The complex also had a madrasa, a hospital, a public kitchen, a bath and a market street of about 200 shops. A fire in 1912 damaged its outer buildings, and a long restoration of the mosque ended in 2023. The quarter around it, Sultanahmet, is named after it.
